research.title: Research
research.description: Papers, long-form essays and technical analyses. Written in paper-mode: serif, numbered sections, citations.

intro.paragraph1: I take the decision nobody finished structuring (what gets built, what doesn't, and which number tells you afterwards whether it worked), write it down with the trade-offs in plain sight, and then build it. Four years at Banana Software, from trainee to product engineer: I led end-to-end projects with teams of three or four, B2C and B2B platforms with payments in the middle, and pulled roughly one in five planned features off the roadmap because they didn't earn what they cost. Sprint predictability went from 60% to 90% once I started modelling real effort.
intro.paragraph2: I'm a bioengineer from ITBA. My thesis predicted 2-year mortality in patients with colorectal cancer liver metastasis, using radiomics and machine learning on real data from Hospital Italiano de Buenos Aires. Before that I was a teaching assistant in Biomedical Image Processing and in Biosensors. It left me in the habit of asking a decision for a number before making it.
intro.paragraph3: Since 2026 I publish analyses of real markets and products, using public data only: <balances>the balance sheets insurers file with the regulator</balances>, <srt>workers' compensation statistics</srt>, <canales>the companies' own digital channels</canales>. Every case ends in a decision: how much money is at stake, what the first step would be, which metrics measure it by segment, and what is not worth building. The figures trace back to their source and the assumptions are declared as assumptions.
intro.paragraph4: I'm looking for a decision analytics role in consulting, or a product role in payments, insurance or health. I work remotely from Argentina with teams in the US and LATAM, and I'll move to Buenos Aires for a hybrid role. If your team has decisions that today get made without numbers, email me. And if it's a product you're thinking about and you want a second head on it, book a call.

tools.intro: I do the analysis in Python and SQL, and the measurement with PostHog. When I need to see the product working, I prototype it in Next.js and TypeScript. I've integrated payments with Stripe, Mercado Pago and PayPal, and moved a product off Bubble to rewrite it in Next.js.

method.title: Method
method.intro: A case study about a real company is advice nobody asked for, so the bar for rigor goes up rather than down. These are the rules every analysis on this site is written under, and what they guarantee when you read one.

sources.title: Where each figure comes from
sources.body: There are three levels of source and each one supports different claims. An archive where the company is a row (the filings it submits to its regulator, the Medicare files, the tables in a 10-K) is the strongest: it allows calculating something nobody published. A figure published by an identifiable third party can be used, but it inherits that party's method, so it comes in with a verbatim quote and a date. And what a company says about itself is data about what that company claims, never about the world: it is written as "the company says that", and it never carries the thesis of a case.

facts.title: No number reaches the text without going through the fact sheet
facts.body: Before the article there is a sheet where every data point enters with three things: the exact value, its status (published figure, own calculation over an official source, press version, or model assumption) and its source. Rounding is declared, assumptions carry the formula and not just the result, and date-dependent data is quoted with its date.

code.title: Calculations are code, not loose numbers
code.body: Everything labelled as my own calculation has a committed script and the download URL of the raw dataset. The links to those scripts are at the foot of each case. A calculation that cannot be rerun is an opinion with decimals.

archive.title: Cited pages are archived
archive.body: Pages change underneath the quote: in one case the source rewrote its table twice while the analysis was in review. So every page cited is archived on the Internet Archive, and the article links the snapshot, not the live page.

audit.title: Every figure is checked before publishing
audit.body: Before it ships, every number in the article, including the ones on the header cards, is cross-checked against the sheet: value, status and source. The internal arithmetic is recomputed. A case publishes when that pass comes back with no high-severity findings, and it gets corrected in public if one shows up later.

decision.title: The recommendation is written so you can judge it
decision.body: Each case ends in a decision, not in a conclusion. It says what decision the company has in front of it, how much money is at stake, what the first step would be, which metrics measure it broken down by segment with the threshold set before looking at the result, what is not worth building, and on what criterion it gets dropped. If it cannot be argued with, it is not a recommendation.

limits.title: What you will not find
limits.body: Figures that cannot be traced back to a source. Assumptions dressed as data: when there is an assumption, it is declared as one. And process narrative: the theses that did not survive and the mistakes that got caught stay in the working log, which is not published.
